splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: The circuits disagreed on whether ERISA and MPPAA require actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability to be locked in as of the end of the plan year, or whether actuaries may select assumptions after that date. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers in multiemployer pension plans. SCOTUS resolved this split.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be selected and fixed by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers greater predictability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that a plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing use of more current data in calculating withdrawal liability.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund v. M & K Employee Solutions

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: The circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the period of court-ordered supervision beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year. SCOTUS resolved this split.

positions.label: Supervised release is tolled during absconding
positions.summary: Holds that the supervised release term is paused while the supervisee is a fugitive, allowing revocation proceedings after the nominal term has expired.

positions.label: Supervised release is not tolled
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory authority for tolling supervised release when a supervisee absconds, and the term expires as originally set regardless of flight.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: The circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face a categorical bar under § 2244(b)(1) on raising any claim previously presented in a successive § 2255 motion, in addition to the separate requirements of § 2255(h). If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement than Congress may have intended. SCOTUS resolved this split.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1) on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, imposing an additional restriction beyond § 2255(h).

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar does not apply to federal prisoners' § 2255 motions; they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: The circuits disagreed on whether candidates can establish Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures like ballot-counting deadlines. The outcome determines whether election administration disputes are resolved before or after elections, with significant practical consequences for mail-in voting rules nationwide. SCOTUS resolved this split.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates suffer a cognizable competitive injury sufficient for Article III standing when a state law changes the rules governing how ballots are counted in their election.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate's generalized interest in election rules does not establish a concrete, particularized injury sufficient for Article III standing absent a more direct harm.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bognet v. Secretary Commonwealth of Pennsylvania

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: The circuits are deeply split on whether 'and' in § 3553(f)(1) means a defendant must meet all three criminal-history criteria to be disqualified from safety-valve relief, or whether meeting any single criterion is disqualifying. This split results in defendants with identical criminal histories being sentenced differently depending on the circuit, with significant liberty implications.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps agency or Sentencing Commission deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous provisions in the Sentencing Guidelines that carry criminal consequences.
splits.description: The circuits are split on whether lenity should prevail over deference to agency or Commission interpretations in criminal sentencing contexts. At least three circuits hold that lenity trumps deference, while the Third Circuit held that deference trumps lenity. The issue has grown more significant after Loper Bright overruled Chevron deference.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes priority over Auer/Kisor deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations in criminal or sentencing contexts, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability through delegated interpretive power.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that Auer/Kisor deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary controls over the rule of lenity when Guidelines provisions are ambiguous, giving the Commission's interpretation binding weight.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses like conspiracy, such that Application Note 1 expanding the definition to include conspiracy exceeds the Sentencing Commission's authority under Kisor v. Wilkie.
splits.description: The circuits are split on whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which adds inchoate offenses (conspiracy, attempt, aiding and abetting) to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is entitled to deference under Kisor/Stinson. Some circuits continue to defer to the note, while others hold the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses. The Commission has since amended the guideline text, but the split remains relevant for cases sentenced under prior versions.

positions.label: Application Note 1 is entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that § 4B1.2(b) is ambiguous and Application Note 1 is a reasonable, authoritative interpretation entitled to controlling weight under Stinson/Kisor, so conspiracy qualifies as a controlled substance offense for career offender purposes.

positions.label: Application Note 1 exceeds guideline text and is not entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously does not include inchoate offenses and Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the guideline's scope, so conspiracy does not qualify as a controlled substance offense.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the substance is controlled under state law but not under the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: The circuits are split on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the underlying substance to be controlled under federal law, or whether a state-law conviction suffices even if the substance is not federally scheduled. This affects career offender and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: State law controls — no federal-schedule requirement
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines broadly define 'controlled substance offense' to include offenses under state law, without requiring the substance to also be controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

positions.label: Federal schedule required
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a controlled substance offense only if the underlying substance is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law (such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)) can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), and whether the Sentencing Commission's policy statement in U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6) authorizing such relief exceeds the Commission's statutory authority.
splits.description: The circuits are split on whether non-retroactive changes in law can serve as extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, and whether the Sentencing Commission may authorize such relief through policy statements. The Seventh and Eighth Circuits have held that non-retroactive changes cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons, while other circuits have been more permissive. The Commission's 2024 amendment to § 1B1.13(b)(6) has intensified the dispute.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons under § 3582(c)(1)(A), and the Sentencing Commission's policy statement purporting to authorize such relief exceeds its statutory authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in law, alone or combined with other factors, can constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for sentence reduction, and the Commission has authority to define such reasons in policy statements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may expressly impose a sentence upon revocation of supervised release to punish the defendant for the violation, or whether revocation sentences must be limited to facilitating the defendant's reentry into the community.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on the permissible purposes of a sentence imposed upon revocation of supervised release. The Sixth Circuit permits district courts to expressly punish defendants for supervised release violations, while other circuits hold that such sentences should serve reentry and rehabilitative goals rather than retributive punishment. This affects hundreds of revocation proceedings annually.

positions.label: Punishment is a permissible purpose
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly impose revocation sentences to punish the defendant for the supervised release violation, in addition to other sentencing goals.

positions.label: Revocation sentences should focus on reentry, not punishment
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release revocation sentences should primarily serve to facilitate the defendant's reentry into the community, and that express reliance on punishment as a justification is improper.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal appeal deadline applies to an order denying a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees filed in a criminal case.
splits.description: The circuits are split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees, though filed in a criminal case, is a civil matter subject to the 30-day civil appeal deadline or a criminal matter subject to the 14-day criminal deadline. The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies because such a motion is ancillary to the criminal case.

positions.label: Civil appeal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under FRAP 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal appeal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that because the Hyde Amendment motion is filed in a criminal case, the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under FRAP 4(b) governs.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a federal prisoner's challenge to BOP decisions regarding the terms or conditions of confinement — such as transfer to prerelease custody under the First Step Act — is properly brought as a habeas corpus petition under 28 U.S.C. § 2241 or as a civil rights action.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether challenges to conditions or terms of confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement) are cognizable in habeas or must be brought through civil rights actions. This split affects how federal prisoners seek judicial review of BOP decisions regarding earned time credits and transfer to halfway houses under the First Step Act.

positions.label: Habeas is available for conditions/terms challenges
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus under § 2241 is available when a prisoner challenges BOP decisions affecting the execution of a sentence, including transfer to prerelease custody, because such challenges relate to the duration or manner of confinement.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: Woodall v. Federal Bureau of Prisons

positions.label: Habeas is not available; civil rights action required
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to conditions or terms of confinement that do not directly affect the fact or duration of imprisonment must be brought as civil rights actions, not habeas petitions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: The circuits are split on whether appreciation in asset value that occurs between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and the conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. The Ninth Circuit holds that such appreciation belongs to the estate, while other circuits have held it belongs to the debtor. This affects debtors' ability to retain home equity gains when converting cases in good faith.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that under the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A) and § 541(a), post-petition appreciation in asset value belongs to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that § 348(f)(1)(A) was enacted to protect good-faith converting debtors, and post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in asset value belongs to the debtor, not the estate.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents referencing private medical treatments and diagnoses is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether denial of a motion to seal medical records in litigation is 'effectively unreviewable' on appeal from final judgment, satisfying the collateral order doctrine's requirements. The D.C. Circuit found such orders immediately appealable given the high-order privacy interest in medical information, while other circuits have taken a narrower view of collateral order jurisdiction for sealing denials.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of 'high order' warranting immediate appellate review, because delayed review risks irreversible disclosure of sensitive medical information.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal are generally not immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine, as parties can seek protective orders or other remedies and appeal after final judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: Circuits have applied differing standards for evaluating discrimination claims in the hospitality and service industry context, leading to inconsistent outcomes. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to clarify standards for fair treatment, discrimination liability, and damages applicable to business operators nationwide.

positions.label: Broader liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a more expansive standard for discrimination claims against business operators, permitting claims based on a wider range of discriminatory conduct.

positions.label: Narrower liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a more restrictive standard for discrimination claims, requiring a higher showing of intentional or systemic discrimination by business operators.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state law categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violates the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and whether as-applied equal protection challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether categorical bans on transgender athlete participation survive intermediate scrutiny when applied to individuals who have undergone medical transition. The case also raises the broader question of whether sex-based classifications affecting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.

positions.label: Categorical ban violates Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that a categorical ban fails intermediate scrutiny as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated biological advantages, because the state has not shown the ban is substantially related to its interest in competitive fairness for this subclass.

positions.label: Categorical ban does not violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that biological sex-based classifications in athletics are substantially related to the important governmental interest in fair competition and the safety of female athletes, even as applied to transgender women.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
